title: Price of bandit information in multiclass learning
formal: For each integer \(k\ge2\), determine up to universal constant factors the largest possible deterministic price of bandit information \[P(k)=\sup\left\{\frac{\operatorname{BLdim}(H)}{\operatorname{Ldim}(H)}:\ X\ne\varnothing,\ \varnothing\ne H\subseteq[k]^X,\ 1\le\operatorname{Ldim}(H)<\infty\right\}.\] The supremum ranges over arbitrary domains and hypothesis classes; \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\) is the allowed label set. The numerator and denominator are the bandit and ordinary Littlestone dimensions defined below. They equal the optimal deterministic worst-case mistake bounds with, respectively, correct/incorrect feedback and full-label feedback in realizable online classification. This is the source’s deterministic realizable question. Its matching-order resolution is \(P(k)=\Theta(k\log k)\).
why: The ratio isolates the cost of receiving only a correctness bit after a prediction, across all realizable multiclass learning problems. Matching upper and lower bounds identify an unavoidable information cost independently of algorithmic speed. The additional logarithm also distinguishes deterministic prediction from the later randomized theory.
status_note: Resolved in the deterministic realizable model at the matching-order scale Θ(k log k): Long 2020 gives the upper bound, Geneson 2021 corrects the lower-bound proof, and NeurIPS 2024 §1.1.1 explicitly states matching bounds for every k≥2. The source asks for BL-dim(H)/L-dim(H); its deterministic scope is preserved. No exact finite-k formula or Lean formalization is claimed.

importance.reason: A class-uniform characterization of the information cost of partial feedback in online learning. The historical resolution separates deterministic and randomized mistake bounds and sharpens the relationship between two central learning dimensions.

sentences: A bandit learner receives only a bit saying whether its predicted label was correct.
The original question compares its best deterministic worst-case mistake bound with the best full-label mistake bound.
These bounds equal bandit and ordinary Littlestone dimension, so the question asks for their largest ratio with k labels.
The corrected literature establishes a ratio of order k log k, while the later randomized model has a different order.
The card is archived as a resolved historical question with its model, matching theorem and proof-correction provenance recorded.

definitions: A hypothesis \(h\in H\) is a function from the instance set to \([k]\). In the full-information game, each round presents an instance \(x_t\), the learner predicts \(\widehat y_t\in[k]\), and it then sees the true label \(h(x_t)\). In the bandit game it instead sees only the bit \(\mathbf1\{\widehat y_t=h(x_t)\}\). The same unknown hypothesis must realize the entire finite sequence. The learner knows the class and may use arbitrary deterministic history-dependent rules, with no running-time, memory, representation or computability restriction. Its mistake bound is the supremum of the number of wrong predictions over all finite horizons, all target hypotheses and all instance sequences. Adaptive choices of instances are allowed; the worst-case bound over all finite sequences already includes them. A bound is independent of horizon, and no expectation or failure probability is involved. A complete binary Littlestone tree of depth \(r\) has an instance at each internal node and two distinct labels on its outgoing edges. It is shattered by \(H\) if each root-to-leaf path has a hypothesis agreeing with every edge label on that path’s instances. \(\operatorname{Ldim}(H)\) is the largest shattered depth. A complete \(k\)-ary bandit Littlestone tree has an instance at each internal node and all \(k\) different labels on its outgoing edges. It is bandit-shattered if each root-to-leaf path has a hypothesis disagreeing with every edge label on that path’s instances. \(\operatorname{BLdim}(H)\) is the largest such depth; an unbounded sequence of depths gives dimension infinity. Initially interpret the supremum and a potentially infinite numerator in the extended nonnegative reals; the known universal upper bound makes \(P(k)\) finite. Dimension-zero classes are excluded from the ratio because they contain only one distinct function and both optimal mistake bounds are zero. Labels in the codomain need not all occur. The requested constants cannot depend on \(k\), the domain, class or either dimension; logarithms may use the natural base since only constant factors are requested.
answer_criterion: A formal completion of this historical question is a Lean-checked proof that there are universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) for which \[c\,k\ln k\le P(k)\le C\,k\ln k\qquad\text{for every integer }k\ge2.\] The upper bound must cover every class in the supremum, and the lower bound must give a class, or approaching family of classes, for each label count. The bound is for deterministic worst-case realizable mistakes. A randomized expected-mistake theorem, an agnostic regret theorem or a bound with a missing logarithmic factor does not prove this statement. This archived record reports the checked mathematical resolution; it does not claim that the cited paper proofs have already been formalized in Lean.

source_formulation.text: For a fixed number of labels, how large can the ratio of bandit to ordinary Littlestone dimension be?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase

context_blocks.text: A full-label learner learns the correct answer even after a mistake. A bandit learner only learns that its guess was wrong, so several other labels can remain plausible. The source compares the strongest deterministic learner in each model, not a particular algorithm and not regret relative to an imperfect comparator.

The source’s ordinary and bandit Littlestone dimensions precisely describe those two optimal mistake bounds. Ordinary shattering permits a path of correct label requirements; bandit shattering requires a hypothesis avoiding each guessed label along a path. Finite ordinary dimension makes the full-information problem learnable, and the resolved comparison bounds the extra mistakes required by reduced feedback.

Long’s upper bound has leading scale \(k\ln k\) times the full-information optimum. Its lower-bound argument contained an incorrect pairwise-independence assertion. Geneson identifies exactly when that assertion fails and supplies a replacement argument recovering the matching lower scale. The archival decision uses the corrected result rather than the original proof alone.

The 2024 NeurIPS paper explicitly states the deterministic result as a universal \(O(k\log k)\) upper ratio and, for every \(k\ge2\), a matching \(\Omega(k\log k)\) example. This directly matches the label-count supremum in the source question. The present card requests that order, not an exact finite-\(k\) value or a new leading-constant optimization.

The same 2024 paper proves a different price of \(\Theta(k)\) when randomization and expected mistake bounds are allowed, with appropriate adaptive and oblivious adversary conventions. That theorem does not replace the source’s deterministic dimension ratio. Keeping the learner model explicit avoids losing the logarithmic factor from the historical answer.
